b: As AI-generated dramas flood our screens, what does their extraordinary rise reveal about the future of storytelling and our insatiable appetite for content?

Two chiseled men escape from prison in the dead of night. Twenty minutes in, one is attacked by a warthog and the other is due to fall pregnant. This is the most popular series on MyMuse, an app specialising in AI-generated microdramas – and I’ve just spent £10 in virtual coins to watch it.

We’ve entered the unhinged era of AI microdramas, essentially soap operas run through the TikTok model: short, vertically filmed episodes, packed with cliffhangers and designed to be watched through a phone screen. In this world, the laws of physics are optional, accents change between scenes and characters rarely blink – except in the one where His Pearl Tears Are Worth Millions. The storylines seem to operate on the principle that if something dramatic can happen, then it absolutely must.

First popularised in China, microdramas have become one of the fastest growing forms of screen entertainment, with the global market projected to reach $14 billion in 2026. Designed for our dwindling attention spans, these low-budget, live-action productions became an unlikely lifeline for actors and film crews struggling to find work following the 2023 Hollywood strikes. But since generative AI reared its head, it has made it possible to churn out an entire series without cameras, actors or narrative coherence, and despite their questionable quality, millions of people are watching. What began as a low-budget alternative to traditional television has become a lucrative experiment in how quickly, cheaply and compulsively entertainment can be produced and consumed.

TikTok has perfected the art of keeping us scrolling, and microdramas have found a way to make us pay for it. Soap operas have relied on dramatic revelations and improbable romances for decades, while lust and longing are ever-present in some of our greatest literature. But microdramas compress these familiar techniques into a relentless cycle of anticipation and reward. Combined with the endless feed of social media and the behavioural tricks of gambling platforms, watching TV begins to operate like a slot machine.

Episodes typically last between one to three minutes, each ending just as a secret is about to be revealed. Desire is a particularly effective lure, with many series blurring the line between drama and soft porn. Free episodes often build towards an encounter that remains tantalisingly out of reach until a paywall appears. Viewers can purchase coins to unlock more episodes, sign up for expensive subscriptions or watch adverts to progress. Either way, these platforms are getting paid.

According to a report by HolyWater Tech, the company behind MyMuse, the formula appears to be working. A staggering 93% of viewers were still watching an hour after subscribing, while the company’s heaviest returning viewers are averaging over 13 hours a week. I too, experienced the primal part of my brain switch on, unable to look away and irrationally desperate to know what happens next. As HolyWater rather ominously put it, we’ve yet to find the ceiling for how much the most dedicated viewers will consume.

What kind of fiction thrives under these conditions? Whether it's billionaire romances, sexually charged rivals or glow-ups of biblical proportions, the same themes appear again and again. Characters seem to exist primarily to betray, seduce or humiliate one another, whilst every moment of relative calm threatens to bring the whole enterprise to a halt in an inexhaustible supply of content that recycles the same fantasies, again and again.

The first wave of AI-generated videos was largely the territory of tech bros experimenting with the limits of technology, but as generative video models become more sophisticated, a growing industry has been emerging around turning those experiments into commercially viable entertainment. The emphasis seems to be less on telling better stories than producing more of them. And the industry isn’t limiting itself to new material, especially when there are opportunities to capitalise on the enduring commercial value of celebrity. Case in point: the Australian soap Neighbours is being recut into AI-assisted microdramas turning Margot Robbie’s old storylines into a new product for our phone screens, exploiting and extracting yet another product from a familiar face. For a technology repeatedly promising to ‘redefine storytelling’ and unleash human imagination, it’s a remarkably unimaginative ambition.

An AI-generated series can currently be produced in just two weeks, compared with 12 for live-action. The most popular apps offer creators an AI production toolkit complete with automated storyboarding, visual sets, voice cloning and dubbing in more than 40 languages. Shortical, a microdrama app rapidly expanding into AI (PSA for the discerning: it’s Israeli-owned), claims its ten highest-earning creators made over $2 million in a single quarter, and promises to turn an idea into a global hit within weeks. For a generation facing increasingly precarious creative careers and questioning whether their work will ever matter, the possibility of making a living this way is hardly insignificant.

As the industry celebrates how few people it takes to make a series today, actors are already losing roles to people who don’t exist, while their replacements appear to have inherited some remarkably familiar beauty standards. The aesthetic that social media spent years encouraging real people to aspire to – the eerily uniform, racially ambiguous, but Western-centred ideal of beauty known as Instagram Face – can now be generated without them. From my own extensive – if regrettable – viewing experience, AI microdramas seem particularly fond of a limited gene pool of doe-eyed women and vaguely Mediterranean-looking men, seemingly plucked from a Love Island casting call. A technology capable of conjuring almost anyone, determined to reproduce the same handful of faces.

Even the peculiar world of celebrity worship is finding ways to dispense with real people. One AI microdrama that found fame through TikTok has amassed over 120M views, with its creator setting up social media profiles for the two leads. Between them, they’ve quickly attracted close to 100K followers, some of whom speak directly to the characters as though they were real. Meanwhile, the person behind them remains entirely invisible, referred to by fans simply as ‘the creator’: a rather grand title in an industry concerned with how little creating its creators need to do.

But there’s a difference between making filmmaking more accessible and making the production of content more efficient. These platforms aren’t just competing with TV, they’re competing with scrolling – during commutes, queues and chores, for every spare moment of our lives. It’s no surprise in this race to produce more, the distinction between having the tools to make anything and having the time, freedom and imagination to create something worth watching is becoming blurred.

Storytelling has never been about arriving at the end of a plot. Long before they were written down, stories have passed between people, carrying their fears, desires, histories and ways of understanding the world. Irish storyteller Clare Murphy speaks of how reflecting on our experiences allows us to turn them into stories, transforming what we’ve lived into knowledge and, when shared, wisdom. More than just a sequence of events, a story is somebody’s attempt to make sense of it all. There are as many ways to tell stories as there are people telling them. Myths and romances have been borrowed and retold but each retelling can bring a new understanding of the world, shaped by the experiences of the person telling it.

AI, on the other hand, can reproduce the patterns of stories without having to make sense of the experiences that gave rise to them. In one rather bleak experiment, researchers asked an AI model to generate over 11,000 stories from 236 different countries. Despite the enormous cultural differences, it repeatedly produced variations of almost exactly the same plot. Remembering the contents of a story isn’t the same as understanding why someone needed to tell it in the first place.

This is more than a theoretical concern. Having watched a frankly concerning number of AI microdramas while researching, I've encountered almost identical scenes with little more than a change of setting. Writer and cultural critic Kyle Chayka has written about how algorithms have spent years pushing creators towards ‘flattened styles’ of similar work. As he puts it, the “fastest route through the AI machine is to get a cliché: what AI produces is fundamentally kitsch”. Combine this with platforms measuring success in views, shares and watch time, and it’s hardly surprising that the results look so alike. The artistic ambition seems to be capped at whatever the algorithm already knows will sell.

A film (or series) however, is rarely the work of a single imagination. The actors, writers and crews being displaced aren’t interchangeable parts of a production line. There is beauty in the number of minds that come together – their personalities, experiences and creative disagreements all shaping what eventually appears on screen. An improvised performance can reveal something about a character the writer hadn’t previously considered. Better yet, human tensions can find their way into the work itself (lest we forget Don’t Worry Darling). The finished product can become something nobody could have imagined at the outset. Regenerating an AI scene to correct distorted faces or disappearing limbs might require effort – not to mention considerable natural resources – but these glitches are problems of execution. The most valuable struggles of storytelling aren’t technical. They’re empty pages, abandoned ideas or moments of uncertainty when a creator has to question what they’re trying to say in the first place. It’s often through that process that something genuinely unexpected emerges, rather than another version of what already exists.
Hayao Miyazaki puts it best: “all important things in the world are a hassle”. An industry determined to eliminate that hassle loses the human experiences that make it worth watching.

China, where microdramas first took off, offers a glimpse of where this all might lead. In the first eight months of 2026 alone, some 430,000 microdramas were released, with more than 90% reporting some use of AI technologies. An extraordinary amount of entertainment, all competing for a place in an already overcrowded attention economy.

As production becomes cheaper and content more abundant, the platforms controlling distribution become more powerful. Research into China’s microdrama industry found that filmmakers often had limited access to audience data, sometimes receiving little more than figures showing whether viewers were still watching three, five or ten seconds into an episode. Filmmakers have always had to satisfy the people financing their work, but they’re also making stories for systems that measure their worth in a few seconds.

There’s a cruel irony to an industry promising to remove the financial barriers to filmmaking, only for the cost of getting anyone to actually watch your film to become the bigger obstacle. Without free promotional support, producers reported that getting a drama seen could mean spending ten times its production budget on marketing, effectively paying to push their episodes into more people’s feeds. In the US, microdrama companies are pouring advertising money into Meta’s platforms, with some dedicating as much as 75% of their budgets to the tech giant. And through all this, Meta benefits twice: collecting advertising revenue whilst the promotional episodes themselves keep audiences scrolling on its platforms.

For all the promises of democratising filmmaking, the power to reach an audience remains concentrated in remarkably few hands. AI might allow more people to make films without major studio blessing, but it does little to free them from the demands of the platforms distributing their work. The tools might be available to everyone, but the audience certainly isn’t.

And what of the audience? Unlike your run-of-the-mill doomscroll where each video is forgotten almost as quickly as it’s watched, I found myself with a growing collection of unfinished stories rattling around my head. Rather than a revolution in entertainment, AI microdramas are the inevitable conclusion of what the internet has been becoming for years: an endless procession of influencers, trends and cultural products competing for the same shrinking sliver of attention. Everything must be immediate and, more importantly, short enough to watch whilst waiting for the kettle to boil.

When every spare moment is swallowed by another, there’s less room for our own minds to breathe. As the industry races to manufacture ever more stories, I wonder what happens to the ones we might have dreamed ourselves.
